# CA1 demonstration course: evidence, retrieval, and reviewed learning materials

This is self-authored synthetic teaching material for a software demonstration. It is not an official course handout, a research result, or a benchmark of any model. Its examples deliberately separate evidence from claims about quality. The notes contain several topics so that the application must select a subset of passages for a request. A successful demonstration does not establish accuracy for real students.

## RAG ingestion and retrieval

RAG ingestion begins with extracting text from an allowed document. The application divides the text into passages and stores each passage with an identifier, document name, and page reference. An embedding service maps passage text to a numeric vector. The passage vector and its source metadata belong together: a vector without its text cannot supply a reader with inspectable evidence. A small overlap between neighboring passages can preserve context at a boundary, although overlap also creates repeated text.

original_unit.heading: Retrieval: How a Learning Objective Selects Evidence
original_unit.text: At request time, the application embeds the learning objective using a compatible embedding configuration. It compares the query vector with stored passage vectors and ranks candidates by similarity. The selected passages accompany the objective in a text-generation request. The generator should use those passages to explain a covered concept or write an answerable exercise. Retrieval supplies external evidence; it does not update the language model's parameters and does not itself prove the final explanation correct.

## Embedding compatibility and index versions

Embedding compatibility concerns the relationship between stored document vectors and a new query vector. Vectors must have the same dimension before their coordinates can be compared. Matching dimensions alone are insufficient: two models can use different semantic spaces while producing the same number of coordinates. A query from one space must not be assumed compatible with passages embedded by another model.

Embedding compatibility and a reviewed text version are different concerns. Reindexing changes the vectors used by future retrieval. It does not retrospectively repair or approve an already generated explanation. The earlier explanation remains associated with its original source passages and generation settings. If a reviewer later edits that explanation, the system creates a new text version. Keeping these histories separate lets an observer distinguish a retrieval configuration change from a correction to teaching content.

## Reviewed text version and learning access

A reviewed text version identifies the exact content a reviewer inspected. Newly generated teaching material begins as a draft. Saving an edit creates a later draft version, and approval applies to the current version. A learning view should show content only when that current version is approved. If someone changes approved text, its new version needs review before it is shown as published learning material. An approval request for an older version should fail instead of approving unseen changes.

For a reviewed text version example, version one is the original generated draft. A reviewer corrects its title or explanation and saves version two. Approval of version two permits the learning view to display that text. A later save creates version three and returns the material to draft. The original version-one evidence should remain inspectable so an evaluator can tell what the generator produced and what a person changed. A technical script exercising these transitions does not supply a human quality judgment.

records.title_or_stem: A course system changes its embedding model and re-runs retrieval so that future searches use vectors from the new model. Later, a reviewer edits the title and explanation of an already generated explanation, saving a new version. Explain (a) which parts must be rebuilt for the embedding change, (b) what happens to the previously generated explanation and its approval status after the edit, and (c) why an approval request aimed at the older version should not succeed. Justify each point using the supplied material.
records.rationale: The reference answer distinguishes re-embedding source passages from resetting approval after a content edit. The multi-part scenario is answerable from the cited excerpts.
records.proposed_revision: For stronger discrimination, supply a concrete before/after state and require the learner to order the changes. Intended demand: medium to hard, not empirically calibrated.

original_unit.stem: A course system changes its embedding model and re-runs retrieval so that future searches use vectors from the new model. Later, a reviewer edits the title and explanation of an already generated explanation, saving a new version. Explain (a) which parts must be rebuilt for the embedding change, (b) what happens to the previously generated explanation and its approval status after the edit, and (c) why an approval request aimed at the older version should not succeed. Justify each point using the supplied material.
original_unit.answer: (a) Changing the embedding model changes the semantic space, so document vectors must usually be rebuilt before new material is generated; the new query vectors must be compatible with the stored passage vectors. A credential replacement alone would not require this, but a model or relevant option change does, and a useful failure message should explain why reindexing is needed rather than silently comparing incompatible vectors. (b) Reindexing does not retrospectively repair or approve an already generated explanation; that explanation stays tied to its original source passages and generation settings. Editing the title or explanation creates a new draft version, so approval now applies only to the current version, and the learning view should show content only when the current version is approved. (c) An approval request for an older version should fail because it would approve changes the reviewer did not inspect; approval must target the current version. The original version-one evidence should remain inspectable so it is clear what the generator produced and what a person changed.
original_unit.explanation: The embedding model change is a retrieval configuration change: vectors from different semantic spaces must not be compared, so document vectors generally need rebuilding, and reindexing does not retroactively approve generated text. The text edit is a content change: saving an edit creates a later draft, approval binds to the current version, and approving an older version would approve unseen changes. These are separate histories.
original_unit.difficulty_reason: The task combines two distinct workflows and requires reasoning about which side of the system each change affects; it also requires explaining why reindexing cannot substitute for re-approval and why approval is version-bound.

original_unit.heading: Citation identifiers versus citation support
original_unit.text: An existing citation identifier only shows that a passage can be found in the recorded source set. It does not show that the passage supports every sentence in an explanation. Assessing support requires reading the cited text and making a content judgment, not just confirming that the identifier is valid. ## Citation support and evidence boundaries

Citation support requires reading the cited text. An existing citation identifier proves that a passage can be found in the recorded source set. It does not prove that the passage supports every sentence in the explanation. For example, a passage saying that human review is required cannot support a generated claim that retrieval always eliminates mistakes. The citation is structurally valid in that example, but the factual conclusion is unsupported.

When assessing citation support, separate three questions. First, does the cited identifier belong to the passages supplied to this generation? Second, does that passage contain the information needed for the claim? Third, does the explanation preserve any conditions or limitations in that information? A program can check the first question mechanically. The second and third require a content judgment. An automated draft must not be described as human-approved merely because its citation identifiers passed validation.

original_unit.stem: A generated explanation says: 'Because human review is required, retrieval always eliminates mistakes.' It cites a course passage that only states human review is required. Explain why the citation identifier is structurally valid but the claim is still unsupported, using this example. Then state what extra judgment is needed beyond checking the identifier.
original_unit.answer: The identifier is structurally valid because it points to a passage that can be found in the recorded source set, so a mechanical check passes. However, the passage only states that human review is required; it does not say retrieval always eliminates mistakes. So the cited text does not support the factual conclusion. Beyond checking that the identifier belongs to the supplied passages, a system or reviewer must judge whether the passage actually contains the information needed for the claim and whether the explanation preserves any conditions or limitations. Those second and third judgments require content judgment, not just identifier validation, so the draft must not be called human-approved merely because its citation identifiers passed validation.
original_unit.explanation: The correct response separates two things: (1) whether the citation identifier is found in the supplied passages, which can be checked mechanically, and (2) whether the cited passage actually contains the information needed for the claim and preserves its conditions. In the example, the passage about human review being required cannot support the stronger claim that retrieval always eliminates mistakes, so the citation is structurally valid but factually unsupported. The extra judgment is a content judgment, not identifier validation.
original_unit.difficulty_reason: The item requires applying the distinction between structural citation validity and content support to a concrete example, then inferring what additional judgment is needed, which involves two connected steps of reasoning.

## Local operation, exports, and deferred media

This prototype is a local development application. A course groups source documents and generated materials. An export should preserve the teaching text and enough citation metadata to inspect its provenance outside the application. A generation evidence export is more detailed than a student handout: it can contain retrieved passages, configuration signatures, revision history, and provider call usage. Exported material should identify whether the current text is draft or approved.

Credentials belong in local configuration and must not appear in handouts, evidence bundles, or screenshots prepared for review. A daily call limit bounds attempts, including attempts that fail. Before a live demonstration, confirm that text and embedding capabilities are configured; this check alone does not prove that the provider accepts the chosen model. Reusing existing local evidence for workflow demonstrations avoids unnecessary new provider calls.

An evidence boundary is crossed when a requested conclusion cannot be derived from the supplied material. Suppose a learner asks for a clinical treatment dosage while the course notes only explain retrieval systems. The notes provide no clinical evidence. The appropriate response is to report insufficient evidence and avoid inventing a dosage or an exercise that presents one as correct. The generator may explain that the relevant source material is missing. A provider outage or malformed response is an operational failure, not a successful refusal based on evidence.

## Embedding compatibility and index versions

Embedding compatibility concerns the relationship between stored document vectors and a new query vector. Vectors must have the same dimension before their coordinates can be compared. Matching dimensions alone are insufficient: two models can use different semantic spaces while producing the same number of coordinates. A query from one space must not be assumed compatible with passages embedded by another model.

An evidence boundary is crossed when a requested conclusion cannot be derived from the supplied material. Suppose a learner asks for a clinical treatment dosage while the course notes only explain retrieval systems. The notes provide no clinical evidence. ## Embedding compatibility and index versions

Embedding compatibility concerns the relationship between stored document vectors and a new query vector. Vectors must have the same dimension before their coordinates can be compared. Matching dimensions alone are insufficient: two models can use different semantic spaces while producing the same number of coordinates. A query from one space must not be assumed compatible with passages embedded by another model.

original_unit.answer: 首先，更换嵌入模型后，旧索引中由旧模型生成的文档向量与新查询向量可能不在同一语义空间，即使维数相同也不能假定兼容，因此需要重建旧索引中的文档向量；如果教学文本被编辑，还应重新生成依赖该文本的索引或向量，使检索内容与当前文本一致。其次，已批准教学文本被编辑后，不能继续默认为已批准状态；应保留初始生成草稿、实际检索文本、不含凭据的生成设置及后续修订，并请人工审核者填写自己的观察与评分，重新确认或批准修改后文本。第三，导出学生讲义与生成证据时，应标明当前文本是草案还是已批准；生成证据可包含检索到的段落、配置签名、修订历史和提供方调用用量，但不得包含凭据。最后，自动测试通过引用结构校验只能说明标识格式有效，不能提供人工质量判断，因此不能把自动测试结果描述为人工批准。
